summary: Defines new RADIUS accounting attributes and new values for an existing attribute to support compulsory tunneling in dial-up networks. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2867 adds RADIUS accounting details for tunnels that an ISP creates for a user. The new records identify when a tunnel or link starts, stops or is rejected.

subtitle: RADIUS accounting values for recording tunnel and tunnel-link events.

tldr.problem: An ISP providing compulsory tunnels needs accounting records for the tunnels and their links, not only for the dial-up session that carries them.
tldr.mechanism: The memo adds six Acct-Status-Type values for tunnel and link start, stop and rejection events. It also defines an attribute identifying the tunnel connection and an attribute counting lost packets on a link.
tldr.outcome: These records let parties compare tunnel usage information. RFC 2867 is Informational and updates RFC 2866.

today: RFC 2867 is Informational and updates RFC 2866. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 2867.

sections.title: Why Tunnel Accounting Is Needed
sections.content:
A voluntary tunnel is created at the user's request. A compulsory tunnel is created by the service provider without the user's action or choice. Providers may need usage data for billing and network planning.

RADIUS Accounting can collect dial-up usage centrally. RFC 2867 extends it with attributes and status values that describe tunnel activity, and it updates RFC 2866.
sections.plainLanguage: A provider may build a tunnel for a user without asking the user to start it. The provider still needs a way to record how that tunnel was used.

sections.title: Six Tunnel Event Values
sections.content:
The new Acct-Status-Type values are Tunnel-Start (9), Tunnel-Stop (10) and Tunnel-Reject (11). Three related values describe a link within a tunnel: Tunnel-Link-Start (12), Tunnel-Link-Stop (13) and Tunnel-Link-Reject (14).

Each value may be used in an Accounting-Request. The memo lists other attributes that SHOULD accompany each event. A tunnel type that can carry only one link does not need separate link events.
sections.plainLanguage: The accounting request can say whether a tunnel or one of its links started, stopped or was refused. This separates the lifetime of a tunnel from the activity inside it.

sections.title: Tunnel Identifiers and Lost Packets
sections.content:
Acct-Tunnel-Connection (type 68) carries an identifier for a tunnel session. Its string format depends on the tunnel type; for L2TP, it may encode the Tunnel ID and Call ID. The exact encoding is implementation-dependent.

Acct-Tunnel-Packets-Lost (type 86) contains a four-octet count of packets lost on a link. It SHOULD be included in a Tunnel-Link-Stop request. The memo says tunnel attributes do not appear in Accounting-Response packets.
sections.plainLanguage: One field identifies the tunnel session. Another reports how many packets were lost on a link when that link stops.

sections.title: Using Records to Audit Service
sections.content:
A corporation and its ISP can each receive records about a user's resource consumption. The corporation can compare its records with the ISP's bill. The memo says fields such as the user name, tunnel connection identifier and tunnel endpoints can help match accounting requests from a network access server and tunnel server.

For L2TP and PPTP, the memo recommends using the Call-Serial-Number in the tunnel connection identifier. It warns that the PPTP field is 16 bits and can wrap, so that number alone may not distinguish calls over a long period.
sections.plainLanguage: Both organizations can keep records and compare them to check a bill. A call number can help match records, but the shorter PPTP number can eventually repeat.

sections.title: What Accounting Traffic Can Reveal
sections.content: The security section notes that someone who captures RADIUS Accounting packets may be able to analyze tunnel connections passively. The memo does not define additional protection in this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone watching accounting packets may learn information about tunnel connections.
